
August 17, 2026 Badlan (Day 6) Underworld-Badland ALE-IB Free-Surface Modeling Lu et al., 2026 (GMD)
========================================================================================================

**Focus:** Interpretation of two related Lu et al. papers and their
implications for developing a scientific manuscript and numerical
experiments with the ASPECT--Landlab coupling framework.

The two papers are best viewed as a progression:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   \text{true free surface}
   \rightarrow
   \text{surface-process coupling}
   \rightarrow
   \text{tectonic--landscape feedback}
   }

The first paper establishes the numerical foundation: a true
free-surface treatment using an Arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian scheme
with an internal boundary (ALE-IB). The second extends the framework to
coupling tectonic deformation with erosion and deposition.

The two papers are:

-  Lu, N., Moresi, L., and Giordani, J. (2026).
   ``A novel ALE scheme with the internal boundary for true free surface simulation in geodynamic models``.
   *Geoscientific Model Development*, 19, 5191--5206. DOI:
   ``10.5194/gmd-19-5191-2026``.
-  Lu, N., Moresi, L., Giordani, J., and Knight, B. S. (2026).
   ``A novel ALE scheme with the internal boundary for coupling tectonic and surface processes in geodynamic models``.
   *Geoscientific Model Development*, 19, 5723--5741. DOI:
   ``10.5194/gmd-19-5723-2026``.

Two-paper conceptual progression
-----------------------------------

.. table:: Scientific progression

   +-------------------+-----------------------+--------------------------+
   | Paper             | Main numerical        | Relevance to             |
   |                   | problem               | ASPECT--Landlab          |
   +===================+=======================+==========================+
   | Lu et al. (2026a) | Stable and accurate   | Surface motion, mesh     |
   |                   | true free-surface     | deformation, stability,  |
   |                   | evolution             | validation               |
   +-------------------+-----------------------+--------------------------+
   | Lu et al. (2026b) | Coupling tectonic     | Two-way                  |
   |                   | deformation with      | tectonic--landscape      |
   |                   | erosion and           | coupling                 |
   |                   | deposition            |                          |
   +-------------------+-----------------------+--------------------------+

The first paper asks:

   Can we accurately move the geodynamic free surface?

The second asks:

   What happens when a moving free surface is simultaneously modified by
   tectonic deformation and surface processes?

For ASPECT--Landlab, the natural next question is:

   How accurately and efficiently can a finite-element geodynamic model
   exchange deformation with a raster landscape-evolution model, and how
   does the numerical coupling itself influence erosion, transport, and
   deposition?

1. Lu et al. (2026a): True free-surface simulation
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Scientific motivation
---------------------

Traditional geodynamic models often use simplified upper boundary
conditions such as free-slip or no-slip. These do not explicitly allow
the Earth's surface to deform as a physical free surface.

The sticky-air approach can represent topography but introduces
additional computational volume and can suffer from marker fluctuations
and the ``drunken sailor`` or ``sloshing`` instability.

The central contribution is:

.. math:: \boxed{\text{ALE--IB = ALE + internal boundary}}

The internal boundary represents the true free surface inside the
computational domain while retaining an upper sticky-air-like region.

Core free-surface update
------------------------

The free surface is represented by mesh nodes on
:math:`\Gamma_{\rm fs}`:

.. math::

   \mathbf{X}^{n+1}
   =
   \mathbf{X}^{n}
   +
   \Delta t\,\mathbf{u}^{n}
   \qquad
   \text{on } \Gamma_{\rm fs}.

This expresses the basic relation:

.. math::

   \text{surface displacement}
   =
   \text{surface velocity}
   \times
   \text{time interval}.

Free-surface update sequence
----------------------------

The numerical workflow can be summarized as:

.. code:: text

   Solve Stokes equations
             |
             v
       Obtain velocity
             |
             v
       Advect free surface
             |
             v
       Resample surface
             |
             v
       Solve Laplace equation
             |
             v
       Propagate mesh displacement
             |
             v
       Update / remesh mesh
             |
             v
       Continue simulation

The mesh displacement is obtained from:

.. math:: \nabla^2 D_z = 0.

The important point for ASPECT--Landlab is that surface deformation must
be propagated into the computational mesh while preserving mesh quality.

Free-surface stabilization
--------------------------

Lu et al. investigate a Free Surface Stabilization Algorithm (FSSA) and
timestep convergence. This is directly relevant to our ``n_substeps``
work.

Two different numerical questions should be separated:

#. Is the free-surface update itself stable?
#. How frequently should the surface-process operator interact with the
   geodynamic operator?

These are related but distinct numerical problems.

Numerical experiments
---------------------

The first paper considers:

-  sinusoidal topography relaxation;
-  Rayleigh--Taylor instability;
-  delamination;
-  rising sphere;
-  subduction.

The sinusoidal relaxation case is especially useful for ASPECT--Landlab
because an analytical solution is available:

.. math::

   w(x,t)
   =
   w(x,0)\exp\left(-\frac{t}{t^*}\right).

This provides a clean validation problem.

The paper also shows that higher-order elements can improve accuracy and
that ALE-IB is robust for strongly asymmetric geometries.

2. Lu et al. (2026b): Coupling tectonics and surface processes
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

The second paper extends the free-surface framework to tectonic--surface
coupling.

The surface evolution equation is:

.. math::

   \frac{\partial h}{\partial t}
   =
   U
   -
   \nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}_r
   -
   \nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}_d,

where :math:`h` is surface elevation, :math:`U` is tectonic uplift,
:math:`\mathbf{q}_r` is fluvial sediment flux, and :math:`\mathbf{q}_d`
is hillslope sediment flux.

For ASPECT--Landlab this can be interpreted as:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   \frac{\partial h}{\partial t}
   =
   u_z
   -
   \nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}_{surface}
   }

Coupling sequence
-----------------

The second paper's coupling workflow is:

#. Solve the Stokes equations.
#. Obtain the velocity field.
#. Evaluate velocity on the surface.
#. Transfer velocity to the surface-process model.
#. Evolve the landscape through erosion and deposition.
#. Transfer the modified surface back to the tectonic model.
#. Remesh the tectonic domain.
#. Continue the simulation.

This is conceptually very close to the ASPECT--Landlab architecture.

Two surfaces
------------

The paper distinguishes between:

.. math::

   T\text{-surface}
   =
   \text{tectonic-model surface}

and:

.. math::

   S\text{-surface}
   =
   \text{surface-process-model surface}.

The conceptual exchange is:

.. code:: text

   ASPECT
      |
      | velocity
      v
   T-surface
      |
      | transfer
      v
   Landlab
      |
      | erosion/deposition
      v
   S-surface
      |
      | transfer back
      v
   ASPECT surface

3. Relevance to the ASPECT--Landlab implementation
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

The major difference from the UWGeodynamics--Badlands implementation is
the spatial-transfer mechanism.

For ASPECT-to-Landlab transfer, the finite-element solution can be
evaluated at Landlab points using deal.II ``RemotePointEvaluation``.

For the reverse direction, the closest Landlab point can be assigned to
an ASPECT surface degree of freedom:

.. math::

   j^*(i)
   =
   \operatorname*{arg\,min}_j
   \left\|
   \mathbf{x}_i^A-\mathbf{x}_j^L
   \right\|^2,

followed by:

.. math::

   \mathbf{u}_i^A
   =
   \mathbf{u}_{j^*(i)}^L.

Therefore, the current ASPECT--Landlab coupling is spatially asymmetric.

.. table:: Spatial transfer comparison

   +--------------------+--------------------+---------------------------+
   | Coupling           | Direction          | Transfer                  |
   +====================+====================+===========================+
   | UWGeo              | Underworld ->      | Cubic spline              |
   | dynamics--Badlands | surface            | interpolation             |
   +--------------------+--------------------+---------------------------+
   | ASPECT--Landlab    | ASPECT -> Landlab  | FE point evaluation       |
   +--------------------+--------------------+---------------------------+
   | ASPECT--Landlab    | Landlab -> ASPECT  | Closest-point assignment  |
   +--------------------+--------------------+---------------------------+

This difference should be explicitly documented in a future manuscript.

4. Connection to the current ``n_substeps`` investigation
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

The second Lu et al. paper divides the tectonic timestep into smaller
surface-process timesteps. This directly connects to our ``n_substeps``
investigation.

Let:

.. math::

   \Delta t_{\rm sub}
   =
   \frac{\Delta t}{N}.

Then total tectonic displacement remains:

.. math::

   \sum_{k=1}^{N}
   U\,\Delta t_{\rm sub}
   =
   N U \frac{\Delta t}{N}
   =
   U\Delta t.

Therefore, changing ``n_substeps`` does not necessarily change the total
tectonic uplift. If the final landscape changes, the difference can
instead result from the frequency of interaction between tectonic and
landscape operators.

The coupling can be represented as:

.. math::

   \mathcal{I}_{A\rightarrow L}
   \rightarrow
   \mathcal{E}_{L}
   \rightarrow
   \mathcal{I}_{L\rightarrow A}.

The central numerical question becomes:

   How does the frequency of tectonic--surface-process coupling affect
   the accuracy and convergence of landscape evolution?

This connects the current ``n_substeps`` work directly to the
literature.

5. What should be reproduced in ASPECT--Landlab?
---------------------------------------------------

Topographic relaxation
----------------------

A first experiment should reproduce the sinusoidal relaxation problem.

Possible tests include:

-  free-surface evolution;
-  hillslope diffusion;
-  fluvial incision;
-  erosion and deposition;
-  sediment redistribution;
-  comparison against an analytical solution.

A useful parameter sweep is:

.. math::

   k_f =
   0,\,
   10^{-6},\,
   10^{-5},\,
   10^{-4}

with a representative hillslope diffusion coefficient.

The purpose is not simply to reproduce the paper, but to establish a
controlled benchmark for the ASPECT--Landlab coupling.

Fluvial erodibility
-------------------

Increasing fluvial erodibility should be examined through:

-  incision depth;
-  longitudinal profile shape;
-  relief;
-  drainage-network development;
-  erosion rate;
-  deposition rate.

This provides a controlled Landlab sensitivity experiment.

Continental collision
---------------------

A collision experiment can investigate:

.. math::

   \text{convergence}
   \rightarrow
   \text{shortening}
   \rightarrow
   \text{crustal thickening}
   \rightarrow
   \text{mountain building}
   \rightarrow
   \text{erosion}
   \rightarrow
   \text{sediment transport/deposition}.

This represents an actively forced tectonic experiment rather than a
purely numerical benchmark.

6. What the papers leave open
---------------------------------

The papers provide a strong foundation but leave several opportunities
for ASPECT--Landlab.

#. The numerical consequences of different coupling frequencies are not
   the central focus.
#. Spatial resolution mismatch between the tectonic and landscape grids
   is not systematically explored.
#. The consequences of different transfer strategies deserve
   quantitative investigation.
#. The coupled framework can be extended toward more explicit sediment
   routing and storage.
#. A rift setting, with simultaneous uplift and subsidence, provides a
   useful complementary application to collision.

7. Proposed manuscript direction
-----------------------------------

The manuscript should not simply state:

   We coupled ASPECT with Landlab.

A stronger manuscript would ask a numerical-scientific question about
the coupling.

Possible titles include:

   **Numerical accuracy and coupling-frequency effects in two-way
   ASPECT--Landlab simulations of tectonic surface evolution**

or:

   **From tectonic deformation to sediment redistribution: numerical
   assessment of two-way ASPECT--Landlab coupling**

The manuscript can be organized into three levels.

Level 1: Numerical verification
-------------------------------

Test whether ASPECT--Landlab reproduces a known free-surface solution.

Use sinusoidal relaxation and measure:

.. math::

   E_{L_2}
   =
   \left[
   \frac{
   \sum_i
   (h_i^{\rm numerical}-h_i^{\rm analytical})^2
   }{
   \sum_i
   (h_i^{\rm analytical})^2
   }
   \right]^{1/2}.

Also measure:

-  maximum topographic error;
-  RMSE;
-  phase error;
-  free-surface displacement;
-  erosion/deposition error.

Level 2: Coupling verification
------------------------------

Add Landlab surface processes and compare:

.. table:: Suggested coupling cases

   +-----------------+------------------------+---------------------------+
   | Case            | Tectonic component     | Landlab component         |
   +=================+========================+===========================+
   | TR-TM           | ASPECT only            | None                      |
   +-----------------+------------------------+---------------------------+
   | TR-D            | ASPECT                 | Hillslope diffusion       |
   +-----------------+------------------------+---------------------------+
   | TR-F            | ASPECT                 | Fluvial erosion           |
   +-----------------+------------------------+---------------------------+
   | TR-FD           | ASPECT                 | Fluvial + diffusion       |
   +-----------------+------------------------+---------------------------+

Level 3: Scientific application
-------------------------------

Potential applications include:

.. table:: Potential scientific experiments

   +-------------------+-----------------------+--------------------------+
   | Experiment        | Tectonic forcing      | Scientific question      |
   +===================+=======================+==========================+
   | Collision         | Compression           | How does erosion modify  |
   |                   |                       | mountain growth?         |
   +-------------------+-----------------------+--------------------------+
   | Rift              | Extension             | How do uplift,           |
   |                   |                       | subsidence, erosion and  |
   |                   |                       | deposition interact?     |
   +-------------------+-----------------------+--------------------------+
   | Sedimentary basin | Uplift/subsidence     | How does tectonic        |
   |                   |                       | deformation control      |
   |                   |                       | sediment routing and     |
   |                   |                       | deposition?              |
   +-------------------+-----------------------+--------------------------+

8. Why a rift experiment may be particularly powerful
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------===

A collision model is useful, but a rift experiment may provide a more
distinct scientific application for ASPECT--Landlab.

In a collision:

.. math::

   \text{convergence}
   \rightarrow
   \text{uplift}
   \rightarrow
   \text{erosion}.

A rift produces both uplift and subsidence:

.. math:: U_{\rm tectonic}(x,y,t)=u_z(x,y,t),

with:

.. math::

   U_{\rm tectonic}>0
   \qquad
   \text{uplift}

and:

.. math::

   U_{\rm tectonic}<0
   \qquad
   \text{subsidence}.

The landscape therefore contains simultaneous sediment sources and
sinks.

The full feedback can be:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   \text{extension}
   \rightarrow
   \text{faulting}
   \rightarrow
   \text{uplift/subsidence}
   \rightarrow
   \text{erosion/deposition}
   \rightarrow
   \text{sediment loading}
   \rightarrow
   \text{tectonic response}
   }

A possible rift question is:

   How does sediment redistribution modify the topographic and tectonic
   evolution of an actively deforming rift system?

9. Sediment routing as a longer-term opportunity
---------------------------------------------------

The Lu et al. framework primarily represents surface processes through
fluvial and hillslope terms.

A more ambitious ASPECT--Landlab model could explicitly track sediment:

.. math::

   \frac{\partial h}{\partial t}
   =
   U
   -
   \nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}_s,

where :math:`\mathbf{q}_s` is sediment flux.

Distinguish sediment supply:

.. math:: Q_s=\text{sediment supply}

from transport capacity:

.. math:: Q_t=\text{transport capacity}.

If:

.. math:: Q_s < Q_t,

sediment can continue to move downstream.

If:

.. math:: Q_s > Q_t,

the excess sediment is deposited.

Conceptually:

.. math::

   Q_{\rm dep}
   \sim
   Q_s-Q_t
   \qquad
   \text{when } Q_s>Q_t.

This moves the framework from a simple erosion model toward a
source-to-sink sediment-routing model.

10. Central research question
---------------------------------

The strongest central question from today's discussion is:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   \text{How does the numerical coupling between tectonic deformation and
   landscape evolution control the predicted evolution of topography,
   erosion, and sediment deposition?}
   }

This can be divided into three questions.

Question 1: Spatial coupling
----------------------------

How does the mismatch between the ASPECT finite-element discretization
and the Landlab raster grid affect transferred tectonic velocity and
landscape evolution?

.. math::

   \mathbf{u}_{ASPECT}
   \rightarrow
   \mathbf{u}_{Landlab}.

Important parameters include:

-  ASPECT mesh resolution;
-  Landlab resolution;
-  relative grid alignment;
-  transfer method;
-  sharpness of tectonic deformation.

Question 2: Temporal coupling
-----------------------------

How does ``n_substeps`` affect the numerical solution?

The working hypothesis is:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   \text{Increasing coupling frequency reduces temporal
   operator-splitting error}
   }

A useful test is:

.. code:: text

   n_substeps =
       1
       2
       3
       5
       10
       20
       40
       80

Measure:

-  final topography;
-  maximum erosion;
-  maximum deposition;
-  cumulative erosion;
-  cumulative deposition;
-  sediment flux;
-  drainage-network metrics.

Question 3: Physical coupling
-----------------------------

How does erosion and deposition feed back onto tectonic deformation?

.. math::

   \text{tectonic deformation}
   \rightarrow
   \text{topography}
   \rightarrow
   \text{erosion}
   \rightarrow
   \text{sediment redistribution}
   \rightarrow
   \text{surface loading}
   \rightarrow
   \text{tectonic response}.

11. Proposed numerical experiment matrix
========================================

.. table:: Proposed ASPECT--Landlab experiment matrix

   +-----------+------------------+------------------+-------------------+
   | E         | ASPECT           | Landlab          | Primary objective |
   | xperiment |                  |                  |                   |
   +===========+==================+==================+===================+
   | E0        | Free surface     | None             | Verify tectonic   |
   |           |                  |                  | free surface      |
   +-----------+------------------+------------------+-------------------+
   | E1        | Free surface     | Diffusion        | Verify hillslope  |
   |           |                  |                  | coupling          |
   +-----------+------------------+------------------+-------------------+
   | E2        | Free surface     | Fluvial erosion  | Verify fluvial    |
   |           |                  |                  | coupling          |
   +-----------+------------------+------------------+-------------------+
   | E3        | Free surface     | Fluvial +        | Full landscape    |
   |           |                  | diffusion        | response          |
   +-----------+------------------+------------------+-------------------+
   | E4        | Collision        | Fluvial +        | Mountain-building |
   |           |                  | diffusion        | feedback          |
   +-----------+------------------+------------------+-------------------+
   | E5        | Rift             | Fluvial +        | Uplift/subsidence |
   |           |                  | diffusion        | and basin         |
   |           |                  |                  | development       |
   +-----------+------------------+------------------+-------------------+
   | E6        | Rift/collision   | Sediment         | Source-to-sink    |
   |           |                  | transport        | evolution         |
   +-----------+------------------+------------------+-------------------+

12. Numerical convergence experiment
---------------------------------------

Define a reference solution:

.. math:: h_{\rm ref}=h_{N_{\rm ref}},

where, for example,

.. math::

   N_{\rm ref}=40
   \quad\text{or}\quad
   80.

Then calculate:

.. math::

   E_h(N)
   =
   \left[
   \frac{1}{A}
   \int_A
   \left(
   h_N-h_{\rm ref}
   \right)^2
   dA
   \right]^{1/2}.

Similarly:

.. math:: E_E(N)=\left|E_N-E_{\rm ref}\right|

and:

.. math:: E_D(N)=\left|D_N-D_{\rm ref}\right|.

The key analysis is whether numerical error decreases toward a converged
solution as ``n_substeps`` increases.

13. Spatial versus temporal coupling error
---------------------------------------------

We should explicitly distinguish two types of coupling error.

Spatial coupling error:

.. math::

   E_{\rm spatial}
   =
   f(
   \Delta x_A,
   \Delta x_L,
   \text{grid alignment},
   \text{transfer method}
   ).

Temporal coupling error:

.. math::

   E_{\rm temporal}
   =
   f(
   \Delta t,
   n_{\rm substeps}
   ).

Therefore:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   E_{\rm total}
   =
   E_{\rm spatial}
   +
   E_{\rm temporal}
   +
   E_{\rm physical}
   }

where ``E_physical`` represents differences caused by changes in the
physical parameterization rather than numerical coupling.

Separating these error sources could make the manuscript substantially
stronger.

    |

Figure 2: Spatial-transfer test
-------------------------------

Compare different ASPECT and Landlab resolutions and grid alignments.

Figure 3: Topographic relaxation
--------------------------------

Compare ASPECT--Landlab against the analytical solution.

Figure 4: ``n_substeps`` convergence
------------------------------------

Plot RMSE, maximum topographic difference, erosion difference, and
deposition difference against ``n_substeps``.

Figure 5: Erosion/deposition
----------------------------

Show topography, erosion, deposition, and sediment flux.

Figure 6: Tectonic application
------------------------------

Show ASPECT velocity, surface elevation, erosion, deposition, and
strain/plasticity for a collision or rift experiment.

Figure 7: Source-to-sink evolution
----------------------------------

Show:

.. code:: text

   uplift
      |
      v
   erosion
      |
      v
   sediment production
      |
      v
   transport
      |
      v
   deposition
      |
      v
   basin filling

15. What would make the manuscript genuinely new?
---------------------------------------------------

The manuscript should avoid presenting the contribution as merely:

   ASPECT + Landlab coupling

because the general concept of coupling geodynamics and landscape
evolution already exists.

The novelty should instead come from one or more of:

#. **A different coupling architecture**

   ASPECT finite-element point evaluation + Landlab raster surface
   evolution.

#. **A quantitative study of spatial-transfer error**

   Especially the consequences of asymmetric ASPECT-to-Landlab and
   Landlab-to-ASPECT transfer.

#. **A quantitative study of temporal coupling**

   ``n_substeps`` as a control on operator-splitting error.

#. **A systematic sediment-routing experiment**

   Moving beyond simple erosion/deposition to explicit sediment
   transport.

#. **A new tectonic setting**

   For example, a rift where uplift and subsidence coexist.

#. **A numerical convergence framework**

   Demonstrating when the coupled solution becomes insensitive to grid
   resolution and coupling frequency.

16. Recommended manuscript hypothesis
---------------------------------------

The most testable hypothesis is:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   \text{The predicted landscape and sediment distribution in a
   two-way ASPECT--Landlab simulation depend systematically on both
   spatial-transfer resolution and temporal coupling frequency.}
   }

A more specific version is:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   \text{As }n_{\rm substeps}\text{ increases, the coupled solution
   approaches a converged tectonic--landscape state, but the convergence
   rate depends on spatial resolution and the transfer method between
   ASPECT and Landlab.}
   }

17. Recommended experiment for immediate implementation
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
A scientifically defensible sequence is:

.. code:: text

   STEP 1
   ------
   ASPECT sinusoidal topographic relaxation
                |
                v
        analytical solution

   STEP 2
   ------
   ASPECT + Landlab diffusion
                |
                v
       numerical convergence

   STEP 3
   ------
   ASPECT + Landlab fluvial erosion
                |
                v
        erosion/deposition

   STEP 4
   ------
   n_substeps = 1 ... 40/80
                |
                v
       temporal convergence

   STEP 5
   ------
   change ASPECT/Landlab resolution
                |
                v
       spatial convergence

   STEP 6
   ------
       tectonic collision or rift
                |
                v
       full scientific experiment

This gives a clean progression from **verification** to **numerical
convergence** to **scientific application**.

18. Key conclusions from today's discussion
---------------------------------------------

The two Lu et al. papers provide a useful roadmap for ASPECT--Landlab.

First, Lu et al. (2026a) establishes that accurate free-surface
evolution requires careful treatment of mesh motion, surface advection,
and timestep stability.

Second, Lu et al. (2026b) demonstrates that when surface processes are
coupled to tectonic deformation, numerical differences in surface
tracking can propagate into erosion and sediment distribution.

Third, the ASPECT--Landlab coupling is numerically distinct from the
Underworld--Badlands implementation because ASPECT-to-Landlab uses
finite-element point evaluation, while the reverse transfer uses
closest-point assignment.

Fourth, this asymmetric spatial transfer creates a natural numerical
research problem.

Fifth, the current ``n_substeps`` investigation provides an equally
important temporal numerical problem: how frequently the tectonic and
landscape operators exchange information.

The coupled problem can therefore be summarized as:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   \underbrace{
   \mathcal{I}_{A\rightarrow L}
   }_{\text{spatial transfer}}
   \rightarrow
   \underbrace{
   \mathcal{E}_{Landlab}
   }_{\text{surface evolution}}
   \rightarrow
   \underbrace{
   \mathcal{I}_{L\rightarrow A}
   }_{\text{spatial transfer}}
   \rightarrow
   \underbrace{
   \mathcal{S}_{ASPECT}
   }_{\text{tectonic evolution}}
   }

with:

.. math::

   \Delta t_{\rm sub}
   =
   \frac{\Delta t_{\rm ASPECT}}
   {n_{\rm substeps}}.

19. Central question to carry forward
------------------------------------------

.. admonition:: Key research question

   **How do spatial and temporal errors in the two-way ASPECT--Landlab
   coupling propagate into predicted topography, erosion, sediment
   transport, and deposition during tectonic landscape evolution?**

This naturally leads to:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   \text{spatial transfer}
   \rightarrow
   \text{temporal coupling}
   \rightarrow
   \text{landscape/sediment response}
   }

The long-term scientific extension is:

.. math::

   \boxed{
   \text{tectonics}
   \leftrightarrow
   \text{topography}
   \leftrightarrow
   \text{erosion}
   \leftrightarrow
   \text{sediment transport}
   \leftrightarrow
   \text{deposition}
   }

This moves the ASPECT--Landlab framework toward a genuinely coupled
tectonic--landscape--sedimentary system.
